opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because I think the old mental model doesn't really carry over. On the human web, the value of a content source was largely measured by attention: did someone click, did they stay, did they see an ad. An agent doesn't behave that way. It might read fifty pages in a second, use three sentences from one of them, and never "visit" in any sense a human would recognize.

So I think the right way to frame it is marginal contribution to the outcome. If you take that source out, how much worse does the agent's answer or action get? Some sources are almost interchangeable. Ten sites say the same thing, and any one of them is fine. Others are uniquely valuable. They have original reporting, proprietary data, a fresh fact nobody else has, or they're the authoritative primary source. Those disproportionately determine whether the agent gets it right.

That has a few implications. First, freshness and originality matter more than ever, because agents are very good at collapsing redundant information. Second, provenance matters. An agent that can trace a claim to a primary source is far more trustworthy than one that blends together a bunch of derivative summaries. And third, and I think this is the important part for the ecosystem, we need economic models that reflect that contribution. If the web is going to be used more by agents than by humans, which I think is where we're heading, then the people creating valuable content have to be compensated in a way that's tied to how much value they actually create for those agents. Otherwise the incentives to produce good, original information erode, and everyone, agents included, ends up worse off.

So the short answer: value is contribution to the quality of the output, and building the infrastructure to measure and reward that is, I think, one of the more important open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response measures value by how much worse the agent’s answer or action becomes without a source and discusses compensation tied to contribution. It does not estimate monetary value using the additional compute cost needed to maintain equivalent output quality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we mostly don't know yet, and that's the problem.

When a human reads the web, there's this whole implicit economy. You visit a page, you see ads, maybe you subscribe, the publisher gets some signal that their work mattered. The value flows, imperfectly, but it flows. When an agent reads the web on your behalf, that loop breaks. The agent pulls from fifty sources, synthesizes something, hands you an answer, and the sources are invisible. Nobody clicked. Nobody saw anything.

So the first thing I'd say is that the value of a content source to an agent's output is real, often decisive, and almost totally unmeasured right now. If the agent gets the right answer because one obscure forum post from 2019 had the exact fix, that post was enormously valuable in that moment. But the system has no way to express that.

The second thing is that value is contextual, not intrinsic. The same source is worth a lot for one query and nothing for another. That's different from how we've historically thought about publisher value, which was about audience size and page views. For agents, the question is closer to: how much did this source change the answer? Did the model already know this, or did this source actually move it? That's a counterfactual question, and it's hard, but I think it's the right frame.

And the third thing, which is the part I find most interesting, is that if you can measure that contribution even roughly, you can start building a different kind of economy. One where content creators get compensated based on how much their work actually improved outcomes, rather than how many eyeballs they captured. That's a healthier incentive than what the attention economy gave us. It rewards being right and being useful over being loud.

I'm not naive about how hard this is. Attribution in a generative system is genuinely messy. But I'd rather be working on the messy version of the right problem than optimizing the clean version of the wrong one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a source’s contextual contribution and asks how much it changed the answer, but it does not estimate monetary value using the extra compute cost of matching output quality without that source.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is contextual. It depends on what the agent is trying to do and what that source contributes to the answer. A source could be broadly useful, but for a particular question, a very niche piece of content might be the most valuable thing the agent can access.

One way to think about it is: what would the output look like without that source? Would it be less accurate, less complete, or impossible to produce? That gets you closer to the source’s contribution than simply counting whether it was retrieved or cited.

The hard part is that sources overlap. If ten sources contain the same information, the information can be essential even though any one source is replaceable. So you have to distinguish the value of the information from the incremental value of a particular source.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how a source affects output quality and whether its information is replaceable, but it does not estimate monetary value using the additional compute cost of achieving equivalent output quality without the source.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to frame it is: how much better does the agent’s answer become because it has access to that source? That’s different from asking how many words it used from the source. A single fact could be essential to getting an answer right, while a large amount of text might add very little.

And that value depends on the task. A source might be valuable because it’s authoritative, because it’s fresh, or because it contains something you can’t find elsewhere. If many sources provide the same information, attributing the value to any one of them becomes harder.

So I’d start with the counterfactual: if the agent didn’t have this content, would its output be less accurate, less useful, or less complete? That’s the contribution you want to understand.

r001.rationale: The response frames value as how much the source improves the answer and asks whether output quality would decline without it. It does not estimate monetary value from the additional compute cost of achieving equivalent output quality without the source.
